reviews.scope: Identifying triangle sides, vertices, and interior angles to match included and opposite elements.
reviews.reason: Applying the law of cosines requires identifying a triangle's sides and interior angles so two sides and their included angle are properly matched with the opposite side.

reviews.scope: Extending the cosine-law identity from special cosine values to general triangle data.
reviews.reason: Evaluating the cosine law at special cosines 0 and 1/2 prepares students for general applications, though general problems can be solved directly from the cosine-law identity without those specific cases.
reviews.counterexample: Recovering an unknown angle cosine from three given side lengths or eliminating cosines between adjacent triangles uses the cosine-law identity directly without evaluating the 0 or 1/2 cases.

reviews.scope: Interpreting cosine values across obtuse angles and exterior turns in triangle geometry.
reviews.reason: The unit-circle definition clarifies cosine signs for obtuse angles and supplementary exterior turns, though many cosine-law tasks supply or recover the cosine algebraically without unit-circle coordinate evaluation.
reviews.counterexample: When side lengths or the angle cosine are given numerically, applying the algebraic cosine law requires no unit-circle coordinate lookup or special-angle evaluation.

reviews.scope: Simplifying radical expressions and real-number calculations when recovering side lengths or cosines.
reviews.reason: Real-number and radical arithmetic supports numerical side-length extraction in the cosine law, but rational-data problems and symbolic cosine eliminations do not require mixed radical operations or rounding.
reviews.counterexample: Finding a rational angle cosine from integer side lengths such as 3, 5, and 7 uses only rational arithmetic without mixed radical operations or decimal approximations.

reviews.scope: Identifying a sphere's center and radius to formulate sphere tangency distance equations.
reviews.reason: Formulating external, internal, and plane tangency equations directly requires knowing what a sphere's center and radius represent as geometric elements of the solid.

reviews.scope: Computing three-dimensional center separations using Cartesian coordinates in sphere contact problems.
reviews.reason: The spatial coordinate distance formula is needed when modeling tangent sphere centers via three-dimensional coordinates, whereas synthetic right-triangle projections solve the same center geometry without coordinates.
reviews.counterexample: Forming a right triangle from the horizontal center distance and vertical center height difference solves for unknown radii or heights via the planar Pythagorean theorem without spatial coordinates.

reviews.scope: Classifying pile sizes by modulo residue classes to prove periodic subtraction-game strategies.
reviews.reason: Modular congruence is required when formulating and proving periodic winning strategies via residue classes, whereas small finite games can be solved directly by explicit backward-induction state tables.
reviews.counterexample: A game with a small finite pile or asymmetric move rules can be completely solved by listing states and applying backward induction from terminal positions without modular arithmetic.
